title: The tonic of wildness
hook: we need the tonic of wildness (Walden 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Walking, read again: the shortest walk in the spirit of undying adventure, and your line, a new walk. Which way did you turn? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

A tonic is a thing you take when you're run down. A bitter little bottle from the druggist's shelf, a spoonful to put the color back in your cheeks. Thoreau reaches for that word in the Spring chapter of Walden, after the ice has broken up on the pond and the sand bank has thawed. But the medicine he prescribes doesn't come in a bottle. It comes from a marsh, a bird call, a place nobody has mapped. And he doesn't say it would be nice to have. He says we need it.
screen: `A BITTER LITTLE BOTTLE.` → `A SPOONFUL WHEN YOU'RE RUN DOWN.` → `THOREAU'S PRESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the line: "We need the tonic of wildness,—to wade sometimes in marshes where the bittern and the meadow-hen lurk, and hear the booming of the snipe." First, the medicine is specific. Not nature as a postcard. Wading. Marshes. Shy birds you hear more than see. Wildness, for Thoreau, is something you get your feet wet in. Second, he wants two things at once. "At the same time that we are earnest to explore and learn all things, we require that all things be mysterious and unexplorable." He's the man who sounded the pond and surveyed fields for a living. And he still needs there to be places that can't be measured. He wants to know everything, and he needs not to. Third, the limits. "We need to witness our own limits transgressed, and some life pasturing freely where we never wander." There's a relief in that. Somewhere, right now, life is going on that has nothing to do with us, our plans, or our town. Seeing that puts us back at our proper size. Fourth, wildness isn't always pretty. In the same passage he describes passing a dead horse near his path, the smell heavy in the air. And even there, he says, he took comfort in nature's strong appetite and its health, a world rich enough to spend lives freely. It's not a comfortable thought. But it's honest. The tonic isn't sweet, and Thoreau takes it anyway, dead horse and all.
screen: `WADE IN THE MARSHES.` · `EXPLORE ALL, YET KEEP THE MYSTERY.` · `OUR OWN LIMITS TRANSGRESSED.` · then, large: `A BITTER TONIC.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch something wild. It doesn't have to be a marsh. A patch of grass. Soil in a pot. A tree's bark. Rain on a window. Wind on your face. If nothing is in reach, remember one wild place you've stood in. Settle and breathe. Rest your hand on it, or your attention. Notice that it isn't yours, and wasn't made for you, and is living anyway. Let that be the tonic for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The tonic of wildness. Thoreau's prescription from the Spring chapter of Walden: marshes, mystery, and life going on beyond our limits. Today's word.
Your line: wildness. Today, find one small patch of the world nobody manages, and give it a minute of your attention without changing anything. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Walden often take the tonic of wildness as a reason to seek out unmanaged places, even small ones, and to let them stay mysterious.
